newsitem.title: USA: Democrat says party in "dire straits," needs cash.
newsitem.headline: Democrat says party in "dire straits," needs cash.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent

The Democratic Party has sent supporters a fund-raising letter written by political strategist James Carville declaring that the party is in "dire" financial straits and could be "crippled for years."
The letter, obtained by Reuters, was sent to 450,000 households across the country. It should start arriving in mailboxes in the next day or two.
"I wanted to take this opportunity to write you about the dire situation our party is in," wrote Carville, who worked for President Bill Clinton's 1992 presidential campaign.

Accusing congressional Republicans of conducting a witch hunt, Carville said their politically inspired investigations of alleged fund-raising misdeeds in the 1996 election had hamstrung Democratic operations.

"Support for the party has dropped in recent months. As a result, our financial resources are drying up fast, forcing us to slow and even stop many of our essential operations," he wrote. "Our party could be crippled for years if we don't do something about it right away," he added, asking supporters to give at least $20 immediately.

Democratic National Committee Chairman Steve Grossman said the party was currently around $16 million in debt and had cut back on what he termed "many non-essential activities" in order to cut costs. But he insisted Democrats would be fully funded and highly competitive in 1998 elections.

"The uncertain environment we've been living through, coupled with a debt left over from the last campaign, makes it incumbent on us to do some very specific things to get ourselves quickly on the road to recovery," he told Reuters.

The Democrats returned some $1.5 million to donors because it suspected the money came from illegal foreign sources and Grossman said it would complete the return of an additional $1.5 million by the end of June..
Clinton, first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton and Vice President Al Gore have pledged to appear at many fund-raising events in the coming months -- 10 this month alone.

Grossman was scathing about the separate investigations being conducted by Senate and House of Representatives committees into the fund raising scandal. The committees were investigating whether China and other foreign interests sought to influence U.S. foreign policy by helping Clinton and the Democratic Party with illegal political contributions.
Grossman said they were spending $16 million of taxpayer money in a "wholly partisan effort to intimidate and paralyse this party."
